articles.label: Public Records
articles.headline: Escambia County spent $47,000 fighting public records requests last year. Here's what they didn't want you to see.
articles.dek: A Flightline analysis of legal fees and denied requests reveals a pattern of resistance to transparency, particularly around code enforcement and property deals.
brief: Escambia County paid outside counsel $47,312 in fiscal year 2025 to review, redact, or deny public records requests
Code enforcement complaints and county property acquisitions generated the most legal pushback
Florida's public records law requires agencies to provide documents unless a specific exemption applies
articles.body:
The invoice arrived in March. Attached: 14 pages of billing entries from Clark Partington, the Pensacola law firm that handles much of Escambia County's outside legal work. The charges documented 47 hours of attorney time spent on a single task—reviewing a records request about a condemned property on West Cervantes Street.

The requester, a neighbor who wanted to know why the county hadn't acted on complaints dating back three years, never got the documents. After two months of waiting and $3,800 in legal review, the county denied the request. Reason cited: ongoing investigation.

That denial was one of 23 the county issued last fiscal year. Together, according to a Flightline analysis of invoices obtained through—yes—a public records request, Escambia County spent $47,312 on outside legal counsel to fight, delay, or heavily redact responses to records requests between October 2024 and September 2025.

The Pattern

Not all records requests cost money. Most don't. Someone asks for a building permit or a meeting agenda, a clerk pulls it, emails it, moves on. The county processes thousands of these annually without incident.

The expensive ones share common traits. They involve code enforcement. Or property transactions. Or communications between commissioners and developers. Or personnel matters in departments that have recently made news.

The Cervantes Street case fits the template. The property, a boarded-up duplex at 2847 W. Cervantes, had accumulated 17 code violations since 2021. Neighbors filed complaints. Inspectors visited. Nothing happened. When Margaret Tillman, who lives two doors down, asked for the inspection reports and any correspondence about the property, the county's public records coordinator forwarded her request to legal.

"I just wanted to know why they weren't doing anything," Tillman told The Flightline. "I've lived here 31 years. I know how this is supposed to work. You file a complaint, they fix it or they fine them. This time, nothing."

What Tillman didn't know: the property's owner, Coastal Investment Holdings LLC, had been in quiet negotiations with the county about a potential sale. The LLC's registered agent is Thomas Bledsoe, a commercial real estate broker whose firm has represented sellers in three county property acquisitions since 2022.

County spokesperson Andrea Mills said the denial was appropriate. "When there's an active code enforcement case that may result in legal action, releasing investigative documents could compromise that process," she wrote in an email. "This is a standard exemption under Florida law."

It is. Florida Statute 119.071 allows agencies to withhold records related to active investigations. But the statute also requires agencies to provide non-exempt portions of documents. Tillman's request included meeting schedules and general correspondence—records that typically don't qualify for exemption.

She received nothing.

Where the Money Goes

The $47,312 figure comes from invoices The Flightline obtained from the County Attorney's office and the Clerk of Court. It represents payments to three outside firms for work specifically coded as "public records review" or "records request litigation."

Clark Partington billed $31,840. Emmanuel Sheppard & Condon billed $11,200. A Tallahassee firm specializing in government law, Nabors Giblin & Nickerson, billed $4,272 for consultation on two requests involving federal grant documentation.

The county's in-house legal staff also spends time on records requests, but those hours aren't tracked separately in budget documents.

For comparison: Santa Rosa County, with a population about 60% the size of Escambia's, spent $8,400 on outside counsel for records-related work during the same period. Okaloosa County spent $12,100.

County Administrator Wes Moreno defended the spending during a budget workshop in April. "We have an obligation to protect confidential information, personnel records, information that could compromise ongoing legal matters," he said. "That review takes time and expertise."

Commissioner Lumon May asked how many requests had resulted in litigation against the county. The answer: one, a case filed in 2024 that was settled for $2,500 plus the requested documents.

"So we spent forty-seven thousand dollars to avoid releasing records, and the one time someone sued us, we lost and had to release them anyway," May said. Moreno did not respond.

The Requests That Triggered Review

The Flightline reviewed 23 denied or heavily redacted requests from fiscal year 2025. They clustered around four topics:

Code enforcement: Nine requests sought inspection reports, violation notices, or correspondence about specific properties. All nine were denied or returned with pages of redactions, citing active investigations. In four cases, the "active investigation" had been open for more than two years with no resolution.

Property acquisitions: Five requests sought appraisals, negotiation records, or communications related to county land purchases. Three were denied entirely. Two were provided with purchase prices and seller names redacted—information that becomes public once a sale closes but was withheld during what the county termed "ongoing negotiations."

Commissioner communications: Four requests sought emails or text messages between commissioners and private parties about development projects. Two were denied as "not public records" because they were sent from personal devices. Two were provided after legal review, with significant redactions.

Personnel matters: Five requests sought records related to employee discipline or departure in the Public Works and Code Enforcement departments. All five were denied, citing personnel exemptions. Florida law does exempt some personnel records but requires disclosure of salary, job title, and dates of employment. In two cases, requesters were told even this basic information could not be provided.

The Legal Framework

Florida's public records law is among the strongest in the country. Article I, Section 24 of the state constitution establishes a right of access to government records. The burden falls on the agency to justify any denial.

But enforcement is left to requesters. If you believe an agency wrongly denied your request, your option is to sue. Most people don't. The cost of litigation—attorneys, filing fees, time—exceeds what most citizens can bear for a code enforcement report or a commissioner's email.

The county knows this. When asked about the low litigation rate, Mills wrote: "The fact that denials are rarely challenged suggests that requesters understand the exemptions are being applied appropriately."

Barbara Petersen, who led the First Amendment Foundation for more than 25 years before retiring in 2021, offered a different interpretation. "A low challenge rate usually means the opposite," she said in a phone interview. "People give up. They don't have the resources to fight, so they walk away. The agency wins by attrition."

What Happens Next

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh proposed a transparency audit during the April workshop, suggesting the county hire an independent reviewer to assess records practices. The motion died without a second.

Commissioner May has since requested a breakdown of legal spending by request type, which the county attorney's office said it would provide "when available."

Meanwhile, the duplex on West Cervantes Street remains boarded up. Margaret Tillman still doesn't know why. The investigation, according to the county, remains active.

"Active," she said. "That word does a lot of work around here."

articles.label: Downtown
articles.headline: The Palafox parking problem nobody wants to solve
articles.dek: Downtown merchants say weekend crowds are killing their businesses. The city says garages sit half-empty. Both are right. The real issue is a 2019 deal that went sideways.
brief: Downtown Pensacola merchants report losing 20-30% of weekend sales due to perceived parking shortages, while city data shows garages rarely exceed 60% capacity
A 2019 public-private partnership with ParkPensacola LLC created a fragmented system where the most convenient spaces are reserved for monthly pass holders
City Council has declined to revisit the contract three times since 2023, citing a $2.1 million early termination penalty
articles.body:
On a Saturday night in May, the Jefferson Street Garage sits three-quarters empty. Five blocks south, a line of cars circles Palafox Street for the third time. Drivers crane their necks at every cross street, hunting for a spot that doesn't exist.

This is the Palafox parking problem. Everyone knows it. Nobody wants to fix it.

"I watch people give up," said Maria Castellanos, who has owned Coastal Provisions on South Palafox for eleven years. "They circle, they circle, they leave. I know because they call me. 'We tried to come for dinner but couldn't find parking.' That's a $200 ticket walking out the door."

Castellanos isn't alone. A survey conducted by the Downtown Improvement Board in March found that 73% of Palafox merchants rated parking as their top business concern. Forty-one percent reported measurable revenue losses they attributed to parking availability.

The city's numbers tell a different story.

Two truths, one garage

According to data provided by the Pensacola Parking Division, the three downtown garages—Jefferson Street, Romana Street, and the Palafox Place structure—averaged 47% occupancy on weekend evenings in 2025. Peak usage topped out at 61% on New Year's Eve.

"We have capacity," said David Thornton, director of the city's Public Works and Facilities department. "The garages are there. They're lit, they're safe, they're patrolled. We can accommodate another 800 vehicles on a typical Saturday night."

Both claims are true. The problem is that truth and usefulness parted ways in 2019.

That's when the city signed a 15-year agreement with ParkPensacola LLC, a subsidiary of Nashville-based Consolidated Parking Solutions. The deal promised to modernize downtown parking infrastructure, install smart meters, and create a unified mobile payment app. In exchange, ParkPensacola would manage all three garages and retain 70% of revenue.

What the deal also did—buried in Section 14.3 of the 97-page contract—was designate the first two floors of each garage as "priority access zones" available exclusively to monthly pass holders.

The floor that isn't there

Monthly passes cost $125 and are sold primarily to downtown office workers. They guarantee a space on levels one and two of any garage, the floors closest to street level with the shortest walks to Palafox.

By 5 p.m. on weekdays, those floors are full. By 6 p.m. on weekends, they're nearly empty—pass holders have gone home. But the spaces remain reserved. Visitors must park on levels three through five, adding two to four minutes of walking time through concrete stairwells or waiting for elevators that serve all five floors.

"It's not that far," Thornton acknowledged. "But perception matters. People see those empty spaces on the lower floors and assume the garage is full. Or they don't want to climb four flights of stairs. I understand that."

The city installed digital signage in 2022 showing real-time availability by floor. The signs are accurate. They're also easy to miss at 25 miles per hour with a car behind you.

What the contract says

The ParkPensacola agreement runs through 2034. Early termination requires the city to pay a penalty equal to three years of projected revenue—currently estimated at $2.1 million based on 2025 figures.

Renegotiating the priority access zones is technically possible but would require ParkPensacola's consent. The company has shown no interest.

"We have a contract," said Brenda Holloway, regional director for Consolidated Parking Solutions, in a phone interview. "The city entered into it voluntarily. The terms were clear. Our pass holders are customers too, and they were promised those spaces."

Holloway noted that monthly pass sales generate approximately $340,000 annually, making them the most profitable segment of downtown parking revenue.

City Council has considered the issue three times since 2023. Each time, it died without a vote.

"The termination penalty is a non-starter," said Escambia County-area Pensacola City Council member Jennifer Alderman. "We're not paying $2 million to get out of a parking contract when we have potholes on Cervantes. That's not a defensible use of public money."

Council member Ray Santiago, whose district includes downtown, disagreed but acknowledged the political reality. "We made a bad deal. But admitting that costs money, and nobody wants to be the one who writes that check."

The surface lot question

Some downtown advocates have proposed an alternative: building a new surface lot on city-owned land near the Community Maritime Park. A 2024 feasibility study identified a 1.2-acre parcel on Main Street that could accommodate 180 spaces at an estimated cost of $1.4 million.

The lot would be city-operated, outside the ParkPensacola contract. It would also be 900 feet from Palafox—farther than the upper garage floors.

"You're solving the wrong problem," said Tom Brennan, executive director of the Downtown Improvement Board. "We don't need more spaces. We need the spaces we have to work better. That means fixing the contract or waiting it out until 2034."

Eight more years.

What merchants are doing

Some businesses have stopped waiting for the city.

Castellanos now validates parking for customers who spend more than $50, eating the $8 garage fee herself. She estimates it costs her $400 a month. "It's cheaper than losing the customer entirely," she said.

The Bodacious Olive, a specialty food shop on Palafox, started offering free bicycle valet on weekend evenings last summer. Owner Kathy Ziegler said it draws a younger crowd that wasn't driving anyway.

"We adapted," Ziegler said. "You wait for the city to fix something, you'll be waiting forever."

Others have been less sanguine. Three restaurants on South Palafox have closed since 2024, citing multiple factors. All three mentioned parking in their public statements.

No easy answers

The parking problem isn't unique to Pensacola. Cities across the country have struggled to balance revenue-generating contracts with street-level accessibility. Austin, Texas bought out a similar agreement in 2021 for $8 million. Cincinnati let its contract expire and spent two years untangling the transition.

Pensacola's contract includes a provision requiring the city to maintain existing meter rates for the duration of the agreement. That means the $1.50 hourly rate on Palafox—unchanged since 2019—can't be raised to push more drivers toward garages. It also can't be lowered to make street parking less attractive during peak hours.

"We locked ourselves in," Santiago said. "Good intentions, bad execution. The city wanted a partner to handle parking so we could focus on other things. Now parking is all anyone wants to talk about."

Thornton, the Public Works director, maintains that the system works as designed. "If everyone used the garages as intended, there would be no problem," he said. "The infrastructure is there. The issue is behavior."

Castellanos has a different view. She was restocking shelves on a Tuesday afternoon, the slow part of the week. A delivery truck blocked the crosswalk outside her window.

"You can't engineer your way out of a bad contract," she said. "And you can't blame customers for not wanting to park in a concrete maze five blocks from where they're going. The city made a deal that made sense on paper. Paper doesn't walk to dinner."

The Jefferson Street Garage, meanwhile, is open 24 hours. Levels three through five have plenty of space.

articles.label: NAS Pensacola
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 200,000 visitors and one question: Who pays for the chaos?
articles.dek: Pensacola Beach braces for its biggest tourism surge of the year while residents and business owners fight over who should foot the bill for traffic control, cleanup and emergency services.
brief: An estimated 200,000 visitors will descend on Pensacola Beach for the Blue Angels homecoming airshow this weekend, generating millions in economic activity
Escambia County and Santa Rosa County split costs for traffic deputies, emergency medical services and post-event cleanup, but residents say the formula is outdated
Beach business owners oppose a proposed tourism surcharge while homeowners push for visitor fees to offset infrastructure strain
articles.body:
The line for Casino Beach parking starts forming at 4 a.m. By sunrise, it will snake past Portofino towers and onto the Bob Sikes Bridge. Deputies will wave cars through intersections where traffic lights become suggestions. Trash cans will overflow by noon.

This is homecoming weekend. The Blue Angels return to Pensacola for their signature show over the Gulf, and the math is familiar: 200,000 visitors, $25 million in estimated economic impact, three days of gridlock on a barrier island with one road in and one road out.

What's less familiar is who writes the checks when it's over.

"Every year we have this same conversation after the fact," said Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh during a budget workshop last month. "And every year we kick the can down the road."

The can has gotten heavier. Escambia County spent $847,000 on traffic control, emergency services and cleanup for last year's homecoming show. Santa Rosa County, which shares jurisdiction over Pensacola Beach through the Santa Rosa Island Authority, contributed $212,000. The Navy covers its own security and operational costs but provides no direct funding to local governments for the civilian side of the event.

The gap between what the show costs and what each entity pays has become a point of contention between beach residents, business owners, county officials and the tourism development council.

The traffic problem nobody wants to solve

Pensacola Beach has roughly 4,500 permanent residents. On homecoming Saturday, the population multiplies by a factor of 40.

The Escambia County Sheriff's Office deploys 85 deputies for traffic control across the three-day event. Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office adds another 30. Most work overtime shifts that start before dawn and end well after the last F/A-18 lands at NAS Pensacola.

"We're not complaining about the work," said ECSO spokesperson Amber Southard. "But the overtime budget for this one weekend exceeds what we spend on some entire months of regular operations."

Last year's overtime bill for ECSO deputies assigned to homecoming: $318,000. The sheriff's office requested a 15% increase for 2026, citing fuel costs and updated pay scales.

Pensacola Beach resident and civic association president Tom & Linda Chen have pushed for a dedicated funding stream since 2019. Their proposal: a $10 vehicle entry fee during major events, collected at the toll plaza and split between traffic enforcement and infrastructure maintenance.

"The people causing the wear and tear should pay for the wear and tear," Tom Chen said. "That's not controversial anywhere else in Florida."

It's controversial here. The Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce opposes any fee that might discourage visitors. Chamber president Shelby Smith called the proposal "a solution looking for a problem" at a March meeting with county staff.

"Our businesses depend on volume," Smith said. "You start nickel-and-diming tourists at the bridge, they'll go to Orange Beach instead."

The cleanup crews and the morning after

By Sunday evening, Casino Beach will have accumulated an estimated 18 tons of trash. Escambia County Public Works crews will work through Monday to clear it. Porta-potties rented for the event will be hauled away. Temporary fencing will come down. The beach will return to something resembling normal by Tuesday.

The county budgeted $156,000 for post-homecoming cleanup in fiscal year 2026. That figure doesn't include sand restoration or repairs to boardwalks and pavilions damaged by foot traffic.

"We find everything out there," said Public Works supervisor Maria Santos. "Coolers, chairs, tent poles. Last year someone left an inflatable kayak."

The Santa Rosa Island Authority handles some maintenance on the beach's core infrastructure but lacks the equipment for large-scale debris removal. SRIA executive director Paolo Ghio said the authority's role is "coordination, not execution" when it comes to major events.

"We facilitate," Ghio said. "The county operates."

That division of labor has frustrated some county commissioners who say SRIA collects lease revenue from beach businesses but contributes little to event management. SRIA's annual budget is funded primarily by those leases and a portion of the bed tax collected on Pensacola Beach.

"They collect the money, we do the work," Commissioner Bergosh said. "At some point that equation needs to balance."

Emergency services strain

Escambia County EMS transported 47 patients during last year's homecoming weekend. Most were heat-related illnesses or minor injuries. Two were cardiac events requiring advanced intervention.

The county stations additional ambulances on the beach during the airshow, pulling units from mainland coverage areas. EMS director Dr. Harold Tate said the reallocation creates response time gaps elsewhere in the county.

"We manage it," Tate said. "But if something major happens in Ferry Pass while all our resources are on the island, we're relying on mutual aid from the city or Gulf Breeze."

Pensacola Fire Department and Gulf Breeze Fire Department both provide mutual aid during homecoming under existing agreements. Neither charges the county for the coverage.

Baptist Hospital operates a first aid tent on the beach during the show, staffed by volunteer nurses and funded through a grant from the Pensacola Blue Angels Association. The association, a nonprofit booster organization, spent $34,000 on medical supplies and volunteer coordination last year.

"We see it as part of supporting the team," said association president retired Capt. James Forrest. "But we're a small organization. There's a limit to what we can absorb."

The economic argument

Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm, estimates homecoming weekend generates $25 million in direct spending. Hotels from downtown to Perdido Key report near-total occupancy. Restaurants book reservation waitlists weeks in advance.

The bed tax collected during homecoming weekend totaled $1.2 million last year, according to Visit Pensacola data. That money flows to the tourism development council, which allocates it primarily to marketing and destination promotion.

By statute, bed tax revenue cannot be used for general government operations like traffic control or emergency services. It can fund "tourist-related infrastructure," but the definition has been contested.

Santa Rosa Island Authority has argued that beach parking improvements and boardwalk repairs qualify. The county attorney's office has taken a narrower view, limiting bed tax spending to projects directly tied to tourism promotion.

"The money is there," said Escambia County budget director Wes Moreno. "The question is whether we can legally use it for what we actually need."

A state legislative fix could clarify the issue. Rep. Michelle Salzman, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said she's open to discussing a local bill but hasn't committed to sponsoring one.

"I'd want to see buy-in from all the stakeholders first," Salzman said. "Right now I'm not sure everyone agrees on what the problem is."

The show will go on

None of the funding disputes will affect this weekend's homecoming show. The Blue Angels will fly their full demonstration over the Gulf on both Saturday and Sunday, weather permitting. Practice sessions on Thursday and Friday will draw their own crowds, smaller but still significant.

NAS Pensacola public affairs officer Lt. Cmdr. Chelsea Brown said the Navy welcomes community feedback on event logistics but emphasized that civilian traffic control is a local government responsibility.

"We partner with local agencies to make this event successful," Brown said. "But our focus is on flight operations and base security."

The partnership, such as it is, will play out this weekend in the usual choreography. Deputies directing traffic at Via de Luna. EMS crews staging near the Gulfside Pavilion. Public Works trucks idling on Quietwater Beach Road, waiting for the crowds to thin.

Come Monday, the bills will arrive. The arguments over who pays them will resume.

"We love the Blue Angels," said beach resident Linda Chen. "We just wish someone would figure out the logistics before the show, not after."
